g.q: This soup ___ delicious. Can I have some more?
g.e: Here taste describes a quality, so it's a non-action (state) verb. We use the present simple, not the continuous.

g.q: Be quiet! The baby ___.
g.e: We use the present continuous for actions happening now, at the moment of speaking.

g.q: My dad usually ___ the shopping on Saturday mornings.
g.e: Usually shows a routine, so we use the present simple. With he/she/it we add -s/-es: does.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
g.e: Believe is a non-action verb, so we don't normally use it in the continuous form.

g.q: We ___ (have) lunch at the moment, so I'll call you back.
g.e: Have means 'eat' here, so it's an action verb and can be continuous: we're having lunch now.

g.q: She ___ (not eat) meat. She's a vegetarian.
g.e: A permanent fact or habit uses the present simple. The negative with she is doesn't + base verb.

g.q: Paolo ___ a lot of coffee. He has four cups a day.
g.e: A habit (four cups a day) uses the present simple: he drinks.

g.q: Shh! I ___ to the radio. It's my favourite song.
g.e: Something happening right now uses the present continuous: I'm listening.

g.q: This cake ___ really good. What's in it?
g.e: Smell describing a quality is a non-action verb, so we use the present simple.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: I am need a new phone.
g.e: Need is a non-action verb: we don't normally use it in the continuous.

g.q: What ___ you ___ (cook)? It smells great!
g.e: The action is happening now, so: What are you cooking?

g.q: My grandmother ___ (not like) spicy food.
g.e: Like is a non-action verb. Negative with she: doesn't like.

v.q: When you cook food in very hot oil, you ___ it.
v.e: Fry = cook in hot oil, like chips. Boil and steam use water, and bake uses the oven.

v.q: Vegetables cooked over boiling water, not in it, are ___.
v.e: Steamed food is cooked by the hot vapour from boiling water. It's a very healthy way to cook.

v.q: Which of these is seafood?
v.e: Seafood is fish and shellfish from the sea, like prawns, mussels and squid.

v.q: Salmon, tuna and swordfish are all types of ___.
v.e: Salmon, tuna and swordfish live in the sea, so they are fish.

v.q: A long, dark purple vegetable used in pasta alla Norma: an a___
v.e: In British English it's an aubergine. Americans say eggplant.

v.q: To cook meat or potatoes in the oven with a little oil: r___
v.e: We roast meat and vegetables in the oven: roast chicken, roast potatoes.

v.q: Lemons and limes taste ___.
v.e: Sour is the sharp taste of lemons and vinegar.

v.q: Food that has been in the freezer is ___.
v.e: Frozen food is kept very cold in the freezer.

v.q: Sushi is often made with ___ fish, which is not cooked.
v.e: Raw means not cooked at all.

v.q: Which one is a fruit?
v.e: Cherries are small red fruit. Beef and duck are meat; mussels are seafood.

v.q: Chicken that is cooked in the oven is r___ chicken.
v.e: We say roast chicken (or roasted chicken).

v.q: Food with a lot of chilli is very s___.
v.e: Spicy (or hot) food has a strong, burning taste, like chilli.

s: I usually have cereal for breakfast, but today I'm eating toast.
My mum is cooking pasta with aubergines tonight.
Do you prefer grilled fish or roast chicken?
I don't like spicy food, but I love fresh seafood.

g.q: Look at those dark clouds! It ___ rain.
g.e: We use be going to for predictions based on something we can see now, like dark clouds.

g.q: A: I'm cold. B: Wait, I ___ close the window.
g.e: We use will for decisions we make at the moment of speaking, like offers to help.

g.q: We ___ my grandparents next Sunday. We've already booked the train.
g.e: We use the present continuous for fixed future arrangements, when the time and plans are already organised.

g.q: Don't worry, I ___ tell anyone your secret. I promise.
g.e: We use will / won't for promises. 'I'm not going' needs 'to' after it.

g.q: I think Italy ___ (win) the match tomorrow.
g.e: After I think we usually use will for predictions based on our opinion.

g.q: My sister has bought some paint. She ___ (paint) her bedroom this weekend. Use going to.
g.e: We use be going to for plans and intentions we have already decided.

g.q: A: The phone's ringing. B: OK, I ___ answer it.
g.e: An instant decision at the moment of speaking: I'll answer it.

g.q: Careful! You ___ drop those plates!
g.e: A prediction based on what we can see now: you're going to drop them.

g.q: I ___ the dentist at 4 o'clock tomorrow. It's in my diary.
g.e: A fixed arrangement with a time and place uses the present continuous.

g.q: Which sentence is a promise?
g.e: We use will for promises: I'll call you tonight.

g.q: I don't think it ___ (snow) tomorrow. Use will.
g.e: With I think / I don't think we normally use will for predictions.

g.q: We ___ (move) house next month. We've already signed the contract. Use the present continuous.
g.e: A fixed plan or arrangement: we're moving.

v.q: Your brother's son is your ___.
v.e: Your brother's or sister's son is your nephew. Their daughter is your niece.

v.q: Someone who always tells the truth is ___.
v.e: Honest people tell the truth. The opposite is dishonest.

v.q: Marco never shares his things or spends money on others. He's really ___.
v.e: In British English, mean means not generous, someone who doesn't like giving or spending.

v.q: The opposite of hard-working is ___.
v.e: Lazy people don't like working. Hard-working people work a lot.

v.q: Your father's new wife, who isn't your mother, is your s___.
v.e: We use step- for family members by a new marriage: stepmother, stepfather, stepbrother.

v.q: Someone who likes giving orders to other people is b___.
v.e: Bossy people always tell others what to do, like a boss.

v.q: Someone who worries a lot and gets nervous easily is ___.
v.e: Anxious people worry a lot.

v.q: Your sister's daughter is your ___.
v.e: Niece = the daughter of your brother or sister. Nephew is the son.

v.q: Someone who loves talking and meeting new people is ___.
v.e: Sociable people enjoy being with other people.

v.q: Someone you can always trust to do what they say is ___.
v.e: Reliable = you can depend on them.

v.q: Someone who never changes their mind, even when they are wrong, is s___.
v.e: Stubborn people don't change their opinion easily.

v.q: Your mother's or father's parents are your g___.
v.e: Grandparents = your grandmother and grandfather.

s: I'm going to spend more time with my grandparents this year.
My brother is very sociable, but my sister is quite shy.
We're having a big family lunch on Sunday.
Don't worry, I'll help you with your homework later.

g.q: I ___ my purse yesterday, but luckily I found it.
g.e: Yesterday is a finished time, so we use the past simple, not the present perfect.

g.q: ___ you ever ___ anything online?
g.e: We use the present perfect with ever to ask about experiences in our life. With you we use have.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: I've paid the bill last week.
I've pay the bill last week.
I paid the bill last week.
g.e: Last week is a finished time, so we need the past simple: I paid.

g.q: She ___ just ___ a new laptop. Look, it's on her desk!
g.e: We use the present perfect with just for very recent actions with a result now.

g.q: We ___ (not save) enough money yet.
g.e: Yet goes with the present perfect in negatives and questions: haven't saved ... yet.

g.q: My grandparents ___ (open) their shop in Bagheria in 1985.
g.e: In 1985 is a finished past time, so we use the past simple.

g.q: I ___ that film three times. It's my favourite!
g.e: Experience up to now, no time said: present perfect.

g.q: When ___ you ___ your car?
g.e: With when we ask about a finished time, so we use the past simple.

g.q: I ___ my homework yet.
g.e: Yet goes with the present perfect in negatives and questions.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: I've been to London last year.
I went to London last year.
I've gone to London last year.
g.e: Last year is a finished time, so we use the past simple.

g.q: ___ you ever lent money to a friend?
g.e: Ever + experience: Have you ever lent...?

g.q: They ___ (already / pay) the bill, so we can go.
g.e: Already goes between have and the past participle.

v.q: If you ___ money from a friend, you must give it back later.
v.e: Borrow = take money from someone for a time. Lend = give money to someone for a time.

v.q: How much do you ___ in your new job?
v.e: You earn money by working. You win money in a competition.

v.q: I can't afford a new bike, so I'm ___ up for one.
v.e: Save up for something = keep money little by little so you can buy it later.

v.q: The money you pay to the government from what you earn is ___.
v.e: Tax is money that people and companies pay to the government.

v.q: I lent Luca ten euros, so he o___ me ten euros.
v.e: If you owe someone money, you have to pay it back to them. With he we add -s: owes.

v.q: Money you borrow from a bank to buy a house: a m___
v.e: A mortgage is a special loan for buying a house or flat. You pay it back over many years.

v.q: If you ___ someone money, you give it to them for a short time.
v.e: Lend = give for a time. Borrow = take for a time.

v.q: Something very expensive is ___.
v.e: A rip-off is something that costs far too much. A bargain is cheap for what it is.

v.q: Money you get from your parents every week is ___.
v.e: Pocket money is what parents give children regularly.

v.q: I want to take 50 euros out of the bank. I'll go to the ___.
v.e: A cash machine (ATM) gives you money from your bank account.

v.q: When you buy something, the shop gives you a piece of paper called a r___.
v.e: A receipt shows what you paid. Be careful: the p is silent.

v.q: If I can't pay for something, I can't a___ it.
v.e: Afford = have enough money to pay for something.

s: I've saved some money, so I'm going to buy a new bike.
Have you ever lent money to a friend?
I spent too much money on clothes last month.
My cousin has just got a new job in Palermo.

g.q: I've lived in Bagheria ___ I was a child.
g.e: We use since with a point in time (since I was a child, since Monday).

g.q: They've been waiting for the bus ___ twenty minutes.
g.e: We use for with a period of time (for twenty minutes, for two years).

g.q: How long ___ English?
g.e: For an activity that started in the past and continues now, we use How long + present perfect continuous.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: I've been knowing her for years.
g.e: Know is a non-action verb, so we use the present perfect simple, not the continuous.

g.q: My hands are dirty because I ___ (work) in the garden all morning.
g.e: We use the present perfect continuous for a long recent activity with a result we can see now.

g.q: She ___ (not see) her cousins since Christmas.
g.e: Present perfect + since shows how long something has (not) happened up to now.

g.q: I've lived in Bagheria ___ 2015.
g.e: Since + a point in time (2015).

g.q: We've known each other ___ ten years.
g.e: For + a period of time (ten years).

g.q: You look tired. ___ you been running?
g.e: Present perfect continuous: Have you been running?

g.q: How long ___ for the bus? Twenty minutes!
g.e: How long + an action that started in the past and continues now: present perfect continuous.

g.q: I ___ (wait) for the bus for 20 minutes! Use the present perfect continuous.
g.e: An action that started in the past and is still going on: I've been waiting.

g.q: She ___ (have) her dog since she was a child. Use the present perfect.
g.e: Have (possess) is a non-action verb, so we use the present perfect simple, not continuous.

v.q: I'm not just tired after the marathon, I'm ___.
v.e: Exhausted is the strong adjective for very tired.

v.q: The film was really scary. I was ___!
v.e: Terrified means very frightened. Delighted means very happy.

v.q: If you are starving, you are very ___.
v.e: Starving is the strong adjective for very hungry.

v.q: It was absolutely ___ yesterday. It was nearly forty degrees!
v.e: Boiling means very hot. Freezing means very cold. With strong adjectives we use absolutely, not very.

v.q: Very angry = f___
v.e: Furious is the strong adjective for very angry. We say absolutely furious, not very furious.

v.q: Very big = e___
v.e: Enormous is the strong adjective for very big. Other examples: huge, gigantic.

v.q: Very, very tired = ___.
v.e: Exhausted is the strong form of tired.

v.q: Very, very hungry = ___.
v.e: Starving is the strong form of hungry.

v.q: Very, very angry = ___.
v.e: Furious is the strong form of angry.

v.q: We can say absolutely ___ but not very ___.
v.e: With strong adjectives we use absolutely, not very: absolutely exhausted.

v.q: Very, very surprised = a___.
v.e: Amazed (or astonished) is the strong form of surprised.

v.q: Very, very small = t___.
v.e: Tiny is the strong form of small.

s: I've been studying English since I was a child.
We were absolutely exhausted after the long walk.
How long have you been living in this flat?
The view from the mountain was absolutely amazing!

g.q: Driving in Palermo is ___ than driving in a small town.
g.e: Long adjectives make the comparative with more + adjective + than.

g.q: This is the ___ road in the whole region.
g.e: To compare one thing with all the others in a group we use the superlative: the most + long adjective.

g.q: The bus is ___ fast as the train.
g.e: To say two things are the same we use as + adjective + as.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: My brother drives carefullier than me.
My brother drives the most carefully than me.
My brother drives more carefully than me.
g.e: Adverbs ending in -ly make the comparative with more: more carefully than.

g.q: It's the ___ (bad) traffic jam I've ever been in.
g.e: Bad is irregular: bad, worse, the worst.

g.q: The more you practise, the ___ (good) you drive.
g.e: The + comparative, the + comparative shows that one thing changes with another. Good is irregular: better.

g.q: The train is ___ than the bus.
g.e: One-syllable adjective: fast → faster.

g.q: This is the ___ traffic jam I've ever been in!
g.e: Bad → worse → the worst.

g.q: Driving in Palermo is ___ than driving in Bagheria.
g.e: Long adjectives use more: more stressful.

g.q: The bus isn't ___ the metro.
g.e: Not as + adjective + as.

g.q: Flying is the ___ (safe) way to travel.
g.e: Superlative of safe: the safest.

g.q: My new bike is much ___ (good) than my old one.
g.e: Good → better → the best.

v.q: A long line of cars that are moving very slowly or not at all is a ___.
v.e: A traffic jam happens when there are too many cars and they can't move.

v.q: A place where roads meet and cars drive round in a circle is a ___.
v.e: At a roundabout, cars go round a circle and take the road they need.

v.q: You get ___ a bus, but you get ___ a car.
v.e: We get on (and off) buses, trains and planes, but we get into (and out of) cars and taxis.

v.q: The ___ was going too fast, so the police stopped him.
v.e: The driver controls the car. A passenger travels in it, and a pedestrian walks.

v.q: A big, fast road between cities: a m___
v.e: In British English a big fast road is a motorway. In Italy it's the autostrada.

v.q: A place where you buy fuel for your car: a ___ station (p___)
v.e: In British English we say petrol station. Americans say gas station.

v.q: A place where you leave your car is a ___.
v.e: Car park = a place to leave your car.

v.q: Long lines of cars that can't move are a ___.
v.e: A traffic jam is when traffic can't move.

v.q: The time of day when everyone travels to work is ___.
v.e: Rush hour = the busiest time on the roads.

v.q: If you drive too fast, the police may give you a ___.
v.e: A fine is money you must pay as a punishment.

v.q: In a car you must always wear a s___ b___.
v.e: A seat belt keeps you safe in your seat.

v.q: A place where you buy petrol is a p___ s___.
v.e: Petrol station (American English: gas station).

s: The train is quicker than the bus, but it's more expensive.
This is the worst traffic jam I've ever seen!
Cycling is the cheapest and healthiest way to get to school.
Please slow down, there's a speed camera on this road.

g.q: I usually go to ___ bed at about eleven.
g.e: We use no article in some fixed phrases: go to bed, go to school, go to work, be at home.

g.q: My aunt is ___ engineer.
g.e: We use a/an with jobs. We use an before a vowel sound: an engineer.

g.q: In general, ___ children love ice cream.
g.e: When we talk about people or things in general, we use a plural noun with no article.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: The moon is very bright tonight.
A moon is very bright tonight.
g.e: We use the with things that are unique, when there is only one: the moon, the sun, the sea.

g.q: I bought a jacket and a scarf. ___ jacket was quite expensive. (Write the article.)
g.e: The first time we mention something we use a/an. The second time we use the.

g.q: I'm hungry. I'd like ___ apple, please. (Write the article.)
g.e: Apple starts with a vowel sound, so we use an, not a.

g.q: I love ___ music, but I didn't like the music at the party.
g.e: Music in general: no article.

g.q: Can you close ___ door, please?
g.e: We both know which door: the.

g.q: My brother is ___ engineer.
g.e: Jobs take a/an. Engineer starts with a vowel sound: an.

g.q: We usually go to ___ bed at 11.
g.e: Go to bed, go to school, go to work: no article.

g.q: ___ moon looks beautiful tonight.
g.e: There is only one moon, so: the moon.

g.q: She plays ___ piano really well.
g.e: Musical instruments take the: play the piano.

v.q: I'm really good ___ maths.
v.e: We say good at / bad at something.

v.q: She's afraid ___ spiders.
v.e: We say afraid of and scared of something.

v.q: Can you wait ___ me after the lesson?
v.e: The verb wait takes for: wait for someone or something.

v.q: We're all very interested ___ history.
v.e: We say interested in something.

v.q: What are you worried ___? (Write the preposition.)
v.e: We say worried about something. In questions the preposition often goes at the end.

v.q: It depends ___ the weather. (Write the preposition.)
v.e: We say depend on something, not depend of.

v.q: I'm very good ___ maths.
v.e: Good at + subject or activity.

v.q: My little sister is afraid ___ spiders.
v.e: Afraid of something.

v.q: We're waiting ___ the bus.
v.e: Wait for someone or something.

v.q: I'm not interested ___ football.
v.e: Interested in.

v.q: Don't worry a___ the test. You'll be fine.
v.e: Worry about something.

v.q: This bag belongs t___ my mum.
v.e: Belong to someone.

s: My sister is very good at music, but she hates maths.
I'm not afraid of spiders, but I don't like snakes.
We usually go to the beach on Sundays in the summer.
Are you interested in learning another language at school?

g.q: You ___ use your phone during the exam. It's against the rules.
g.e: Mustn't means it is prohibited, not allowed.

g.q: Tomorrow is Sunday, so I ___ get up early.
g.e: Don't have to means it isn't necessary. Mustn't means it is not allowed.

g.q: You look tired. I think you ___ go to bed earlier.
g.e: We use should to give advice or say what we think is a good idea.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: She has to wear a uniform.
She have to wear a uniform.
She must to wear a uniform.
g.e: With she we say has to. Must never changes and is followed by the base verb without to.

g.q: Yesterday I ___ (have to) wait an hour at the doctor's.
g.e: Must has no past form, so for past obligation we use had to.

g.q: You ___ (should / not) eat so many sweets. Write the negative.
g.e: Shouldn't + base verb gives negative advice: it's not a good idea.

g.q: You ___ use your phone in the exam. It's not allowed.
g.e: Mustn't = it's not allowed (prohibition).

g.q: It's Sunday tomorrow, so I ___ get up early.
g.e: Don't have to = it isn't necessary.

g.q: You look ill. You ___ see a doctor.
g.e: Should gives advice.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: She must to wear a uniform.
She has to wear a uniform.
She have to wear a uniform.
g.e: Has to + base verb. Must is never followed by to.

g.q: Yesterday I ___ (have to) work late. Use the past.
g.e: The past of must / have to is had to.

g.q: You ___ (not / should) talk loudly on the phone on the train.
g.e: Negative advice: shouldn't.

v.q: I tried to call you, but you didn't ___.
v.e: Pick up = answer the phone. Hang up = end the call.

v.q: The battery is nearly dead. I need to ___ my phone.
v.e: You charge your phone to put power back in the battery.

v.q: When you end a phone call, you ___.
v.e: Hang up = end a phone call.

v.q: Sorry, I missed your call. I'll ___ you back later.
v.e: Call someone back = phone someone who phoned you before.

v.q: A short written message you send from your phone: a t___
v.e: A text (or text message) is a short written message. The verb is text too: I'll text you.

v.q: The sound your phone makes when someone calls you: a r___
v.e: A ringtone is the sound or music your phone plays when someone calls.

v.q: When you finish a phone call, you ___.
v.e: Hang up = end a call.

v.q: I couldn't talk, so I'll ___ him later.
v.e: Call back = phone again later.

v.q: A short written message on a phone is a ___.
v.e: Text (message) = a short written message.

v.q: Please put your phone on ___ in the cinema.
v.e: On silent = the phone makes no sound.

v.q: When the phone rings, you p___ u___ to answer.
v.e: Pick up = answer the phone.

v.q: The sound your phone makes when someone calls is the r___.
v.e: Ringtone = the sound of an incoming call.

s: You mustn't use your mobile phone in the cinema.
I don't have to wear a uniform at my school.
You should switch off your phone when you're studying.
Sorry, I missed your call because my phone was on silent.

g.q: I'd love ___ speak Chinese one day.
g.e: Can has no infinitive, so after would love we use to be able to.

g.q: When she was five, she ___ swim, but she couldn't ride a bike.
g.e: For general ability in the past we use could. Was able needs to after it.

g.q: The museum was closed, but luckily we ___ visit the cathedral.
g.e: For one specific success in the past we use was/were able to (or managed to), not could.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: I haven't been able to sleep well lately.
I haven't could sleep well lately.
I haven't can sleep well lately.
g.e: Can has no present perfect form, so we use have been able to.

g.q: I ___ (will / not / be able to) come to the party next Saturday.
g.e: Can has no future form, so we use will be able to. Negative: won't be able to.

g.q: Sorry, I ___ (can / not) hear you. The music is too loud.
g.e: The negative of can is can't or cannot, followed by the base verb.

g.q: When I was five, I ___ swim.
g.e: Past ability: could.

g.q: I'd love to ___ speak Japanese.
g.e: After would love to we need an infinitive: be able to.

g.q: Sorry, I ___ come to your party on Saturday.
g.e: Present or future inability: can't.

g.q: I've never ___ ski.
g.e: After have we need been able to: I've never been able to ski.

g.q: Will you ___ (be able to) help me tomorrow?
g.e: Will + be able to for future ability.

g.q: The test was hard, but I ___ (manage / pass) it. Use was able to.
g.e: For a specific success in the past we often use was able to.

v.q: The lesson was so ___ that I nearly fell asleep.
v.e: Adjectives with -ing describe the thing that causes the feeling: a boring lesson.

v.q: I was really ___ when I heard the news.
v.e: Adjectives with -ed describe how a person feels: I was surprised.

v.q: This homework is really ___. I don't understand it.
v.e: The homework causes the feeling, so we use the -ing adjective: confusing.

v.q: Which sentence is correct?
v.e: To say how a person feels we use the -ed adjective: interested in.

v.q: We were ___ (frighten) during the storm. Use -ed or -ing.
v.e: It describes how we felt, so we use the -ed adjective: frightened.

v.q: That was an ___ (embarrass) mistake! Use -ed or -ing.
v.e: The mistake causes the feeling, so we use the -ing adjective: embarrassing.

v.q: The film was so ___ that I fell asleep.
v.e: -ing describes the thing: a boring film.

v.q: The children were ___ because it was raining all day.
v.e: How people feel: bored. The rainy day was boring.

v.q: Roller coasters are ___!
v.e: The thing that causes the feeling: terrifying.

v.q: I'm ___ in history. It's my favourite subject.
v.e: How I feel: interested.

v.q: The journey was very long and t___.
v.e: The journey causes tiredness: tiring.

v.q: I can't wait for my holiday! I'm so e___.
v.e: How a person feels: excited (not exciting).

s: I was really disappointed because I couldn't go to the concert.
Will you be able to help me with my homework tomorrow?
The film was so boring that I fell asleep.
When I was little, I couldn't swim, but now I can.

g.q: When I arrived at the stadium, the match ___ already ___.
g.e: We use the past perfect for an action that happened before another past action.

g.q: She ___ in the park when she hurt her ankle.
g.e: We use the past continuous for a longer action in progress when a shorter action happened.

g.q: The team ___ three goals by half-time.
g.e: By + a past time often needs the past perfect: the goals happened before half-time.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: While I was watching the match, the lights went out.
While I watched the match, the lights were going out.
While I had watched the match, the lights went out.
g.e: The long action in progress is past continuous (was watching); the short action that interrupted it is past simple.

g.q: He was tired because he ___ (train) hard all morning. Use the past perfect.
g.e: The training happened before he was tired, so we use the past perfect.

g.q: It ___ (rain) when the race started, so the track was wet. Use the past continuous.
g.e: The past continuous describes the background situation when something happened.

g.q: When I arrived, the match ___. I missed the first goal!
g.e: An action before another past action: past perfect.

g.q: It ___ when we left the stadium.
g.e: Background action in progress: past continuous.

g.q: She ___ her leg while she was skiing.
g.e: A short completed action in the past: past simple.

g.q: I didn't play because I ___ my boots at home.
g.e: Leaving the boots happened before: past perfect.

g.q: What ___ you ___ (do) at 8 o'clock last night?
g.e: An action in progress at a time in the past: past continuous.

g.q: By the time we got to the beach, the sun ___ (go) down.
g.e: Before another past moment: had gone.

v.q: In tennis and volleyball, the ball has to go over the ___.
v.e: The net is in the middle of the court in tennis and volleyball.

v.q: A football match is played on a ___.
v.e: Football is played on a pitch. Tennis is played on a court, and golf on a course.

v.q: The person who controls a football match and gives yellow cards is the ___.
v.e: The referee makes sure the players follow the rules. The coach trains the team.

v.q: We ___ the match three to one and went home happy.
v.e: We win a match or a competition. We beat another team: we beat Palermo.

v.q: To get a goal: s___ a goal
v.e: We say score a goal or score a point.

v.q: A big place where people watch football matches: a s___
v.e: A stadium is a large sports ground with seats for fans.

v.q: In football, the person who controls the match is the ___.
v.e: Referee = the official who makes sure players follow the rules.

v.q: The person who trains a team is the ___.
v.e: Coach = trainer.

v.q: We ___ the match because we ___ the other team 3–1.
v.e: We win a match or a race. We beat a person or a team.

v.q: A place where people play tennis is a tennis ___.
v.e: Tennis court. Football is played on a pitch.

v.q: Italy b___ France 2–0. (They won against them.)
v.e: Beat a team. Past simple: beat.

v.q: When a player gets hurt, they get i___.
v.e: Injured = hurt in an accident or while playing.

s: We were losing at half-time, but we won in the end.
When I got to the pool, the race had already started.
She was training for a marathon when she hurt her knee.
The referee blew the whistle and the players ran onto the pitch.

g.q: I ___ play football, but now I prefer basketball.
g.e: Used to + base verb describes past habits that are not true now.

g.q: Did you ___ have long hair when you were a teenager?
g.e: In questions and negatives with did, we write use to without -d.

g.q: I ___ go to the gym on Mondays and Wednesdays.
g.e: For present habits we use usually + present simple. Used to is only for the past.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: We not used to have a car.
We didn't used to have a car.
We didn't use to have a car.
g.e: The negative is didn't use to + base verb, without -d on use.

g.q: My grandfather ___ (use to / work) at the fish market in Palermo.
g.e: Used to + base verb describes a past habit or situation that has finished.

g.q: We ___ (not / use to) have mobile phones at school.
g.e: The negative of used to is didn't use to, with no -d after use.

g.q: I ___ play the piano, but I stopped when I was 12.
g.e: Past habit that doesn't happen now: used to.

g.q: Did you ___ have long hair?
g.e: In questions and negatives: did you use to...?

g.q: I ___ get up early. Now I love it!
g.e: Negative: didn't use to.

g.q: Now we ___ go out on Fridays. (present habit)
g.e: For present habits we use usually + present simple, not used to.

g.q: My grandad ___ (use to / work) in a factory.
g.e: Past habit or state: used to + base verb.

g.q: We ___ (not / use to) have a car.
g.e: Negative: didn't use to + base verb.

v.q: My brother and I ___ very well. We never argue.
v.e: Get on (well) with someone = have a good, friendly relationship.

v.q: Someone you work with is a ___.
v.e: A colleague is a person you work with. A classmate is in your class.

v.q: Luca and I had a big argument yesterday. We ___ about football.
v.e: Fall out (with someone) = argue and stop being friendly.

v.q: After school we ___ in touch, and we still talk every week.
v.e: Keep in touch = continue to contact someone. Lose touch = stop being in contact.

v.q: To meet someone and learn more about them: ___ to know (g___)
v.e: Get to know someone = spend time with them and learn what they are like.

v.q: A friend you know very well and trust: a c___ friend
v.e: A close friend is someone you know very well and trust.

v.q: When two people decide to marry, they get ___.
v.e: Engaged = they have agreed to marry.

v.q: When a relationship ends, the couple ___.
v.e: Break up = end a relationship.

v.q: I ___ well with my sister. We never argue.
v.e: Get on (well) with someone = have a good relationship.

v.q: Someone you know a little, but who isn't really a friend, is an ___.
v.e: Acquaintance = a person you know, but not well.

v.q: Marco and Sara have been g___ o___ together for two years. (dating)
v.e: Go out with someone = have a romantic relationship.

v.q: We had an argument and f___ o___. Now we don't speak.
v.e: Fall out (with someone) = argue and stop being friends.

s: I used to see my cousins every summer when I was a child.
My best friend and I get on really well.
We didn't use to have a computer at home.
I usually meet my friends in the square on Saturday evenings.

g.q: This film ___ in Sicily in the 1950s.
g.e: It's a finished past action and the film didn't do the action, so we use the past simple passive: was made.

g.q: The actors ___ by a famous photographer at the moment.
g.e: Present continuous passive: am/is/are + being + past participle, for something happening now.

g.q: A new cinema ___ next to the station next year.
g.e: Future passive: will be + past participle. The cinema doesn't build anything itself.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: The tickets have already been sold.
The tickets has already been sold.
The tickets have already be sold.
g.e: Present perfect passive: have/has + been + past participle. Tickets is plural, so have.

g.q: The film ___ (direct) by a young Italian woman. Use the past simple passive.
g.e: Past simple passive: was/were + past participle. We use by to say who did the action.

g.q: Many foreign films ___ (dub) into Italian. Use the present simple passive.
g.e: Present simple passive: am/is/are + past participle. Films is plural, so are.

g.q: The film ___ in Sicily last year.
g.e: Past simple passive: was + past participle.

g.q: Popcorn ___ in most cinemas.
g.e: Present simple passive: is sold.

g.q: A new cinema ___ in our town at the moment.
g.e: Present continuous passive: is being built.

g.q: The tickets ___ already ___.
g.e: Present perfect passive: have been sold.

g.q: The winner ___ (announce) tomorrow. Use will.
g.e: Future passive: will be + past participle.

g.q: Romeo and Juliet ___ (write) by Shakespeare.
g.e: Past simple passive with by + the person who did it.

v.q: The person who tells the actors what to do is the ___.
v.e: The director is in charge of making the film and tells the actors what to do.

v.q: The words at the bottom of the screen that translate what people say are ___.
v.e: Subtitles translate the dialogue so you can watch a film in its original language.

v.q: A short video that shows parts of a new film to advertise it is a ___.
v.e: A trailer is a short advert for a film, shown before it comes out.

v.q: All the actors in a film are the ___.
v.e: The cast are the actors. The crew are the people who work behind the camera.

v.q: A film that continues the story of an earlier film: a s___
v.e: A sequel continues the story. For example, part two of a film is a sequel.

v.q: The music of a film: the s___
v.e: The soundtrack is all the music you hear in a film.

v.q: The people who watch a film or a play are the ___.
v.e: Audience = the people watching.

v.q: A film with lots of fights and car chases is an ___ film.
v.e: Action films are full of exciting physical scenes.

v.q: The words at the bottom of the screen that translate the film are ___.
v.e: Subtitles translate the dialogue.

v.q: The music of a film is the ___.
v.e: Soundtrack = the music in a film.

v.q: All the actors in a film are the c___.
v.e: The cast = the actors.

v.q: A short advert for a new film is a t___.
v.e: Trailer = a short preview of a film.

s: The film was shot on a beautiful island near Sicily.
In Italy, many foreign films are dubbed into Italian.
The actors were chosen after a long audition.
The new cinema will be opened by the mayor next month.

g.q: She's shivering and wearing a heavy coat. She ___ be cold.
g.e: We use must when we are almost sure something is true, because of the evidence.

g.q: He ___ be a doctor. He's only fifteen!
g.e: We use can't when we are almost sure something is not true.

g.q: I'm not sure where Anna is. She ___ be at the library.
g.e: We use might (or may, could) when something is possibly true but we are not sure.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
g.e: For deduction the opposite of must is can't, not mustn't.

g.q: The lights are on, so they ___ (must / be) at home.
g.e: The lights are evidence, so we are almost sure: must + base verb.

g.q: I'm not sure, but it ___ (may / not / be) his phone.
g.e: May not / might not = it's possible that it isn't true.

g.q: She's wearing a wedding ring. She ___ be married.
g.e: We're almost sure it's true: must.

g.q: He ___ be 18. He looks about 12!
g.e: We're almost sure it's not true: can't.

g.q: I'm not sure where Anna is. She ___ be at the gym.
g.e: Possible but not certain: might (or may / could).

g.q: Which sentence means 'I'm sure it isn't true'?
o: It might not be his car.
g.e: For deduction we use can't, not mustn't.

g.q: They're not answering. They ___ be asleep. (possible)
g.e: Possibility: might / may / could.

g.q: You've been walking all day. You ___ be exhausted! (sure)
g.e: Logical certainty: must.

v.q: You use your ___ to smell things.
v.e: You smell with your nose. Lips are part of your mouth.

v.q: The part of your body that joins your hand to your arm is your ___.
v.e: Your wrist joins your hand and arm. Your ankle joins your foot and leg.

v.q: When you ___ your head, it usually means no.
v.e: Shake your head = move it from side to side (no). Nod = move it up and down (yes).

v.q: You ___ your hands when you want to show you liked a show.
v.e: Clap your hands = hit them together to show you liked something.

v.q: You have ten of these on your hands: f___
v.e: Fingers are on your hands. The ones on your feet are toes.

v.q: The part in the middle of your leg that bends: your k___
v.e: Your knee is the joint in the middle of your leg. Remember: the k is silent.

v.q: You use your ___ to smell.
v.e: Nose = the part of the face for smelling.

v.q: The joint in the middle of your arm is your ___.
v.e: Elbow is in the arm; knee is in the leg.

v.q: You ___ your eyes when the sun is very bright.
v.e: When the light is too bright we close our eyes.

v.q: When something is funny, you ___.
v.e: Smile when you're happy. Frown when you're worried. Yawn when you're tired.

v.q: You have ten t___ on your feet.
v.e: Fingers on your hands, toes on your feet.

v.q: The part between your head and your shoulders is your n___.
v.e: Neck.

s: She keeps rubbing her eyes, so she must be tired.
He can't be at school today because it's Sunday.
They might be at the beach, but I'm not sure.
My shoulders and back hurt after carrying that heavy bag.

g.q: If you ___ hard, you'll pass the exam.
g.e: First conditional: if + present simple, will + base verb. We don't use will after if.

g.q: I'll call you as soon as I ___ home.
g.e: After time words like when, as soon as, until and before we use the present, not will, for the future.

g.q: You won't get into university ___ you get good marks.
g.e: Unless means if not: you won't get in if you don't get good marks.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: I'll wait here until you come back.
I'll wait here until you will come back.
I wait here until you will come back.
g.e: After until we use the present simple for the future, and will in the main clause.

g.q: If it ___ (rain) tomorrow, we won't go to the beach.
g.e: In the if clause of the first conditional we use the present simple: if it rains.

g.q: We'll start the lesson when everyone ___ (arrive).
g.e: After when we use the present (not will) to talk about the future. Everyone takes a singular verb.

g.q: If you study hard, you ___ the exam.
g.e: First conditional: if + present, will + verb.

g.q: I'll call you when I ___ home.
g.e: After when (future time clause) we use the present simple.

g.q: We won't start ___ everyone is here.
g.e: Until = up to the time when.

g.q: You won't improve ___ you practise.
g.e: Unless = if not.

g.q: If it ___ (rain) tomorrow, we'll stay at home.
g.e: First conditional: if + present simple.

g.q: As soon as the lesson ___ (finish), I'll go to the beach.
g.e: After as soon as we use the present simple for the future.

v.q: If you ___ an exam, you don't pass it.
v.e: Fail is the opposite of pass. Take an exam = do an exam.

v.q: A school that parents pay for is a ___ school.
v.e: Parents pay for a private school. State schools are paid for by the government.

v.q: In Italy, most students aged fourteen to nineteen go to ___ school.
v.e: Secondary school comes after primary school, for teenagers.

v.q: Before an exam, you ___ everything you have studied.
v.e: Revise = study again what you have learnt, to prepare for an exam.

v.q: To behave badly in class: m___
v.e: Misbehave = behave badly. The prefix mis- means badly or wrongly.

v.q: A person who teaches at a university: a l___
v.e: At university, teachers are usually called lecturers or professors.

v.q: The person who is in charge of a school is the ___.
v.e: Head teacher (headmaster/headmistress).

v.q: You ___ an exam if you get a good mark.
v.e: Pass = get a good enough result.

v.q: If you don't pass, you ___ the exam.
v.e: Fail an exam.

v.q: A school where students sleep and live is a ___ school.
v.e: Boarding school = students live there.

v.q: Students at university go to l___ (big talks by a professor).
v.e: Lecture = a talk to a large group of students.

v.q: Another word for taking an exam again: r___ it.
v.e: Retake (or resit) an exam.

s: If I pass my exams, I'll go to university in Palermo.
I'll text you as soon as I get home.
You won't improve unless you practise every day.
We can't start the test until the teacher arrives.

g.q: If I ___ a lot of money, I'd buy a house by the sea.
g.e: Second conditional: if + past simple, would + base verb, for imaginary situations.

g.q: If I were you, I ___ look for a cheaper flat.
g.e: If I were you, I would... is a common way to give advice.

g.q: If it's sunny tomorrow, we ___ have lunch in the garden.
g.e: This is a real possibility in the future, so we use the first conditional: if + present, will.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: If I would live alone, I'd be lonely.
If I lived alone, I'll be lonely.
If I lived alone, I'd be lonely.
g.e: Second conditional: past simple after if, would in the other clause. No would after if.

g.q: What would you do if you ___ (find) a wallet in the street?
g.e: It's an imaginary situation, so we use the past simple after if.

g.q: If we had a garden, we ___ (get) a dog. Use would.
g.e: In the second conditional the result clause uses would + base verb.

g.q: If I ___ rich, I'd buy a house by the sea.
g.e: Second conditional: if + past simple (were is also correct).

g.q: If I were you, I ___ tell her the truth.
g.e: Advice with if I were you: would.

g.q: What ___ you do if you won the lottery?
g.e: Imaginary situation: would.

g.q: Which is a real possibility?
o: If it rains, we'll stay in.
If it rained, we'd stay in.
g.e: First conditional = real/likely future. Second = imaginary/unlikely.

g.q: If we ___ (have) a garden, we'd get a dog.
g.e: Second conditional: if + past simple.

g.q: I ___ (not live) with my parents if I had a job. Use would.
g.e: Second conditional result: wouldn't + verb.

v.q: The area on the edge of a city where many people live is the ___.
v.e: The suburbs are the residential areas around a city, outside the centre.

v.q: The room at the top of a house, under the roof, is the ___.
v.e: The attic is under the roof. The basement is under the ground.

v.q: The top part of the inside of a room is the ___.
v.e: The ceiling is inside the room above you. The roof is the outside top of the building.

v.q: In the UK, a flat on the ___ floor is at street level.
v.e: In British English the floor at street level is the ground floor. The first floor is above it.

v.q: A small outside area on an upper floor of a building: a b___
v.e: A balcony is a small outside area where you can stand or sit, outside a window or door.

v.q: Money you pay every month to live in someone else's flat: r___
v.e: Rent is the money you pay to the owner to live in their house or flat.

v.q: The room under the roof of a house is the ___.
v.e: Attic = room under the roof. Basement = room under the ground.

v.q: A flat where you live in a big building is in a block of ___.
v.e: Block of flats.

v.q: The person who owns the flat you rent is the ___.
v.e: Landlord = owner. Tenant = person who rents.

v.q: A room with a lot of light is ___.
v.e: Bright = full of light.

v.q: A small comfortable room is c___.
v.e: Cosy = warm and comfortable.

v.q: The money you pay every month to live in a flat is r___.
v.e: Rent.

s: If I had a bigger bedroom, I'd invite my friends more often.
If I were you, I'd rent a flat near the city centre.
Our house has a small garden and a balcony upstairs.
What would you do if you won a lot of money?

g.q: I enjoy ___ with people.
g.e: After enjoy we use the -ing form (gerund).

g.q: She decided ___ a new job.
g.e: After decide we use to + infinitive.

g.q: He's very good at ___ problems.
g.e: After a preposition, like at, we always use the -ing form.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: I'd like to work in marketing.
g.e: After would like we use to + infinitive.

g.q: I can't afford ___ (buy) a new car.
g.e: After afford we use to + infinitive.

g.q: Would you mind ___ (close) the door?
g.e: After mind we use the -ing form.

g.q: I enjoy ___ with children.
g.e: Enjoy + -ing.

g.q: We hope ___ our own business one day.
g.e: Hope + to + infinitive.

g.q: I'm good at ___ problems.
g.e: After a preposition (at) we use -ing.

g.q: They let me ___ early yesterday.
g.e: Let + person + base verb (no to).

g.q: I'd like ___ (work) abroad one day.
g.e: Would like + to + infinitive.

g.q: He gave up ___ (smoke) last year.
g.e: Give up + -ing.

v.q: She lost her job because the company didn't have enough work. She was ___.
v.e: Be made redundant = lose your job because the company doesn't need you any more.

v.q: When you stop working because you are old, you ___.
v.e: Retire = stop working at the end of your career. Resign = decide to leave a job.

v.q: The money you get every month for doing your job is your ___.
v.e: A salary is the money you earn for your job. A pension is money you get after you retire.

v.q: She works ___ a nurse at the hospital.
v.e: We use work as + a job: she works as a nurse.

v.q: To tell your boss officially that you are leaving your job: r___
v.e: Resign = officially leave your job because you choose to.

v.q: When you get a better, more important position in your company, you get a p___.
v.e: A promotion is a move to a higher position, often with a better salary.

v.q: If you lose your job because the company has no work, you are made ___.
v.e: Made redundant = lose your job because it's no longer needed.

v.q: When you stop working because you're old, you ___.
v.e: Retire = stop working at the end of your career.

v.q: When you decide to leave your job, you ___.
v.e: Resign = leave your job by choice.

v.q: A job for only some hours a week is a ___ job.
v.e: Part-time = fewer hours than a full working week.

v.q: To ask for a job in writing, you a___ for it.
v.e: Apply for a job.

v.q: A document listing your education and experience is your C___.
v.e: CV (curriculum vitae). American English: résumé.

s: I really enjoy working with children, so I want to be a teacher.
She decided to apply for a job in a hotel.
I'm thinking of looking for a new job next year.
My uncle retired last year after working in a bank for many years.

g.q: 'I'm tired,' she said. She said she ___ tired.
g.e: In reported speech the tense usually goes one step back: am/is becomes was.

g.q: 'We'll call you tomorrow.' They said they ___ call me the next day.
g.e: In reported speech will becomes would.

g.q: 'Where do you live?' He asked me where ___.
g.e: In reported questions we use normal word order (subject + verb) and no do/did.

g.q: 'Are you coming?' She asked me ___ I was coming.
g.e: For reported yes/no questions we use if (or whether).

g.q: 'I bought a new jacket.' He told me he ___ (buy) a new jacket. Use the past perfect.
g.e: In reported speech the past simple usually becomes the past perfect: had bought.

g.q: 'I can't find my keys.' She said she ___ (can / not) find her keys. Move the tense back.
g.e: In reported speech can becomes could, so can't becomes couldn't.

g.q: 'I'm tired,' she said. → She said she ___ tired.
g.e: Reported speech: present → past (is → was).

g.q: 'I'll help you,' he said. → He said he ___ help me.
g.e: Will → would.

g.q: 'Where do you live?' → She asked me where ___.
g.e: Reported questions use normal word order: where I lived.

g.q: 'Are you hungry?' → He asked me ___ hungry.
g.e: Yes/no questions: if / whether + normal word order.

g.q: 'I bought a new dress.' → She said she ___ (buy) a new dress.
g.e: Past simple → past perfect.

g.q: 'Can you help me?' → He asked if I ___ help him.
g.e: Can → could.

v.q: If a shirt is too small, you can take it back to the shop and get a ___.
v.e: A refund is when the shop gives you your money back.

v.q: The piece of paper that shows what you bought and paid is a ___.
v.e: A receipt shows what you paid. Keep it if you want to take something back.

v.q: The noun from deliver is ___.
v.e: Some verbs make nouns with -y: deliver, delivery.

v.q: The noun from complain is ___.
v.e: The noun from complain is complaint. You make a complaint when you are not happy.

v.q: Make a noun from choose: c___
v.e: The noun from choose is choice. It's irregular, so learn it!

v.q: Make a noun from improve: i___
v.e: Many verbs make nouns with -ment: improve, improvement; pay, payment.

v.q: A shop that sells medicine is a ___.
v.e: Chemist's (pharmacy).

v.q: The noun from 'deliver' is ___.
v.e: Deliver → delivery.

v.q: The noun from 'complain' is ___.
v.e: Complain → complaint.

v.q: When something is cheaper than usual, it's in the ___.
v.e: In the sale = reduced price.

v.q: The noun from 'choose' is c___.
v.e: Choose → choice.

v.q: When you take something back to the shop and get your money back, you get a r___.
v.e: Refund = money given back.

s: The shop assistant said the shoes were in the sale.
She asked me if I wanted to pay by card.
I'd like to make a complaint about this delivery.
He told me he had lost the receipt.

g.q: If I ___ the bus, I wouldn't have met you.
g.e: Third conditional: if + past perfect, would have + past participle, for imaginary past situations.

g.q: If she had studied more, she ___ the exam.
g.e: In the third conditional the result clause uses would have + past participle.

g.q: We ___ lost if we had taken the map.
g.e: The situation is imaginary and in the past, so we use wouldn't have + past participle.

g.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: If you would have told me, I would have helped.
If you had told me, I would have helped.
If you told me, I would have helped.
g.e: We use the past perfect after if in the third conditional, not would have.

g.q: If it hadn't rained, we ___ (go) to the beach.
g.e: Third conditional result: would have + past participle. Go becomes gone.

g.q: I wouldn't have been late if my alarm ___ (ring).
g.e: The if clause of the third conditional uses the past perfect. Ring, rang, rung.

g.q: If I'd left earlier, I ___ the train.
g.e: Third conditional: would have + past participle.

g.q: If she ___ me, I would have helped her.
g.e: Third conditional: if + past perfect.

g.q: We wouldn't have got lost if we ___ a map.
g.e: If + past perfect: had had.

g.q: Which sentence is about the past?
o: If I had time, I'd go.
If I'd had time, I'd have gone.
If I have time, I'll go.
g.e: The third conditional talks about an imaginary past.

g.q: If you ___ (study), you would have passed.
g.e: If + past perfect.

g.q: I ___ (not / meet) my wife if I hadn't gone to that party.
g.e: Result: wouldn't have + past participle.

v.q: We were very ___. We found the last two tickets for the concert!
v.e: After be we need an adjective, not an adverb. Lucky means good things happen to you by chance.

v.q: ___, nobody was hurt in the accident.
v.e: We use an adverb (-ly) at the start to comment on the whole sentence. It's good news, so fortunately.

v.q: The opposite of patient is ___.
v.e: Adjectives starting with p often take the prefix im-: impatient, impossible, impolite.

v.q: The adjective from comfort is ___.
v.e: Many adjectives end in -able: comfortable, reliable, enjoyable.

v.q: Make an adverb from careful: c___
v.e: We usually make adverbs by adding -ly to the adjective: careful, carefully.

v.q: The opposite of honest: d___
v.e: We can make opposites with the prefix dis-: honest, dishonest.

v.q: The adverb of 'lucky' is ___.
v.e: Lucky → luckily.

v.q: The opposite of 'fortunate' is ___.
v.e: Fortunate → unfortunate.

v.q: The adjective from 'danger' is ___.
v.e: Danger → dangerous.

v.q: The adjective from 'comfort' is ___.
v.e: Comfort → comfortable.

v.q: The opposite of 'patient' is i___.
v.e: Patient → impatient.

v.q: The adverb of 'careful' is c___.
v.e: Careful → carefully.

s: If I hadn't missed the train, I wouldn't have met my best friend.
Luckily, we found a free table near the window.
If you had told me, I would have helped you.
Unfortunately, it rained all day, so we stayed at home.

g.q: I haven't got ___ time today.
g.e: Time is uncountable, so we use much in negatives and questions.

g.q: There are ___ apps on my phone. I never use most of them.
g.e: Apps are countable, so we use too many to say more than we need.

g.q: There's ___ milk in the fridge. We need to buy some.
g.e: Hardly any means almost none, so we need to buy more.

g.q: This room isn't ___ for all the students.
g.e: Enough goes after an adjective: big enough, old enough.

g.q: I've only got a f___ friends in this town, but they're great.
g.e: A few is used with plural countable nouns and means a small number.

g.q: I spend t___ much time on my phone. I need to stop!
g.e: Too much means more than is good. We use it with uncountable nouns like time.

g.q: There isn't ___ milk left.
g.e: Uncountable nouns: much.

g.q: I've got ___ friends in London.
g.e: Countable plural: a few.

g.q: There are ___ people here. It's really crowded!
g.e: Too many + countable plural.

g.q: We don't have ___ time to finish.
g.e: Enough + noun.

g.q: Could I have a ___ sugar in my coffee, please? (a small amount)
g.e: A little + uncountable noun.

g.q: I've got ___ homework tonight! (a large amount, uncountable)
g.e: A lot of / lots of for large amounts.

v.q: You use a ___ to change TV channels from the sofa.
v.e: A remote control lets you change channels and the volume without touching the TV.

v.q: You connect this to your phone to give the battery power: a ___
v.e: A charger puts power back into your battery.

v.q: To make the music louder, you ___.
v.e: Turn up = make louder. Turn down = make quieter. Turn off = stop it.

v.q: Before you can play a new game on your phone, you usually need to ___ it.
v.e: Download = copy something from the internet onto your device.

v.q: To connect a device to the electricity: ___ it in (p___)
v.e: Plug in = connect a device to the electricity. The opposite is unplug.

v.q: Small devices you put in your ears to listen to music: e___
v.e: Earphones (or earbuds) go in your ears. Headphones go over your ears.

v.q: To put a device in so it gets electricity, you ___ it in.
v.e: Plug in = connect to electricity.

v.q: The small device you use to change the TV channel is the ___.
v.e: Remote control.

v.q: To put a phone's battery back to full, you ___ it.
v.e: Charge a phone.

v.q: To copy a file from the internet to your device, you ___ it.
v.e: Download = from the internet to your device.

v.q: The thing you use to charge your phone is a c___.
v.e: Charger.

v.q: To start using a website with your password, you l___ i___.
v.e: Log in (or log on).

s: I spend too much time on my phone every day.
There aren't enough plugs in this room for all our chargers.
Could you turn the volume down a little, please?
Hardly any of my friends use a desktop computer now.

g.q: She's the singer ___ won the competition.
g.e: We use who (or that) for people.

g.q: That's the café ___ we first met.
g.e: We use where for places.

g.q: My uncle, ___ lives in London, is a chef.
g.e: This is a non-defining clause (with commas), so we can't use that. For people we use who.

g.q: He's the actor ___ brother is a famous footballer.
g.e: We use whose for possession: the actor's brother = the actor whose brother.

g.q: Palermo, ___ is the capital of Sicily, has a famous market. Write the relative pronoun.
g.e: In a non-defining clause (with commas) we use which for things and places, not that.

g.q: This is the book ___ I told you about. Write one relative pronoun.
g.e: For things in defining clauses we use that or which. Here we can also leave it out.

g.q: That's the singer ___ won the competition.
g.e: Who for people.

g.q: This is the town ___ I was born.
g.e: Where for places.

g.q: The phone ___ I bought last week is broken.
g.e: Which (or that) for things.

g.q: She's the woman ___ son plays for Palermo.
g.e: Whose = of whom (possession).

g.q: My brother, ___ lives in Rome, is a doctor. (non-defining, person)
g.e: In non-defining clauses we use who, not that.

g.q: Rome, ___ is the capital of Italy, is beautiful. (non-defining, thing/place)
g.e: Non-defining clauses use which (never that).

v.q: A person who writes songs is a ___.
v.e: Songwriter is a compound noun: song + writer. Many compound nouns are written as one word.

v.q: A person you admire and want to be like is a ___ model.
v.e: A role model is someone you look up to, whose example you want to follow.

v.q: Which word makes a compound noun with sun: sun___?
v.e: Sunglasses protect your eyes from the sun. Other examples: sunscreen, sunset.

v.q: A shop that sells books is a ___.
v.e: In compound nouns the first word describes the second: a bookshop is a shop for books. A library lends books.

v.q: The day you celebrate every year because you were born on that day: your b___
v.e: Birthday is a compound noun: birth + day.

v.q: The title in big letters at the top of a newspaper story: a h___
v.e: Headline is a compound noun: head + line.

v.q: A room where you sleep is a ___.
v.e: Bed + room = bedroom.

v.q: Glasses you wear to protect your eyes from the sun are ___.
v.e: Sun + glasses = sunglasses.

v.q: A place where you can sit and drink coffee is a ___.
v.e: Compound noun: the first word describes the second: a coffee shop.

v.q: Someone you share a flat with is a ___.
v.e: Flat + mate = flatmate.

v.q: The yearly celebration of the day you were born is your b___.
v.e: Birth + day = birthday.

v.q: A small book with your photo that you need to travel abroad is a p___.
v.e: Passport.

s: My grandmother is the person who I admire most in the world.
This is the town where my favourite singer was born.
The film, which was made in Sicily, won lots of prizes.
She is a great role model for young people.

g.q: You're from Bagheria, ___?
g.e: A positive sentence has a negative tag with the same auxiliary: you're ... aren't you?

g.q: She didn't see the thief, ___?
g.e: A negative sentence has a positive tag: didn't ... did she?

g.q: They've already arrested him, ___?
g.e: The tag uses the same auxiliary as the sentence: they've (have) ... haven't they?

g.q: I'm late, ___?
g.e: The question tag for I am is aren't I. It's irregular.

g.q: The police will catch him, ___? Write the question tag.
g.e: With will in a positive sentence the tag is won't. We use they for the police.

g.q: He stole a bike, ___? Write the question tag.
g.e: For past simple positive sentences, the tag is didn't + subject pronoun.

g.q: You're Italian, ___?
g.e: Positive sentence → negative tag.

g.q: She doesn't eat meat, ___?
g.e: Negative sentence → positive tag.

g.q: They went to the party, ___?
g.e: Past simple positive → didn't they?

g.q: You can swim, ___?
g.e: Can → can't you?

g.q: He's been to London, ___? (tag)
g.e: Present perfect positive (he's = he has) → hasn't he?

g.q: It isn't raining, ___? (tag)
g.e: Negative → positive tag: is it?

v.q: A person who breaks into houses to steal things is a ___.
v.e: A burglar enters a house or building to steal. A shoplifter steals from shops.

v.q: Someone who sees a crime happen is a ___.
v.e: A witness sees a crime and tells the police what happened.

v.q: The police ___ him for stealing a car.
v.e: Arrest someone for a crime = take them to the police station. We say accuse someone of, not for.

v.q: Which verb means 'take something from a shop without paying'?
v.e: Shoplift = steal from a shop. The person is a shoplifter.

v.q: The person in court who decides the punishment: a j___
v.e: The judge controls the trial in court and decides the punishment.

v.q: Someone who steals from people's pockets or bags in the street: a p___
v.e: A pickpocket steals from pockets and bags, often in crowded places.

v.q: Someone who takes things from shops without paying is a ___.
v.e: Shoplifter.

v.q: Someone who breaks into houses to steal is a ___.
v.e: Burglar.

v.q: A person who sees a crime happen is a ___.
v.e: Witness.

v.q: The police ___ the thief and took him to the police station.
v.e: Arrest = take someone to the police station because they may have committed a crime.

v.q: A person the police think may have committed a crime is a s___.
v.e: Suspect.

v.q: Someone who steals from people's pockets or bags is a p___.
v.e: Pickpocket.

s: The police arrested the burglar outside the house, didn't they?
You saw the man who stole the bike, didn't you?
The witness told the police exactly what she had seen.
It wasn't easy to catch the pickpocket, was it?
